title: The Kabbalist Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi
content:
The Kabbalist Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi

This source surveys the life and teachings of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi, an exemplary figure who bridged the Kabbalistic traditions of Yemeni Jewry with the mystical world of Jerusalem in the twentieth century. The text describes his personal life trajectory, from his early orphanhood in Yemen to his becoming the elder of the Kabbalists and founder of Yeshivat Nahar Shalom in Jerusalem, while emphasizing his spiritual leadership that combined asceticism and self-mortification with deep social engagement and concern for the needy. Alongside the biographical description, the source details his practical Kabbalistic method based on the kavvanot of the Rashash, his adamant opposition to practical Kabbalah, and his literary legacy including innovative prayer books and books of segulot. The purpose of the composition is to illuminate the Rabbi's decisive influence on Israeli public life and his work in making accessible the wisdom of the esoteric to all strata of the people as a tool for spiritual rectification and redemption.

The Flame of the Esoteric in Jerusalem: The Kabbalistic Teaching, Public Work, and Spiritual Leadership of the Kabbalist Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi

The Dawn of His Life in Yemen and the Foundations of His Education

The figure of the Yemeni Kabbalist, Rabbi Mordechai Yehudah Yifet Sharabi (known universally as Rav Mordechai Sharabi), represents one of the most magnificent spiritual bridges that connected the esoteric traditions of Yemeni Jewry with the world of Jerusalem Kabbalists in the twentieth century.[1, 2] The year of Rabbi Sharabi's birth in the city of Ta'izz in Yemen is subject to slight historical dispute, with sources ranging between the year 5668 (approximately 1908) and the year 5672 (approximately 1912).[1, 3] The dawn of his childhood was suffused with extremely harsh family tragedies, which left him orphaned from both parents at a tender age.[4, 5] His father, Rabbi Yehudah, passed away on the seventh day of Pesach even before his son came into the world, and after only two years, also on the seventh day of Pesach, his mother, Mrs. Miriam, died.[4, 5]

The orphaned child grew up and was educated under the guardianship of his paternal grandfather, the Kabbalist Rabbi Avraham Yifet Ta'izi, who served as head of the rabbinical court in the city of Ta'izz.[6, 7] The grandfather, who identified in his grandson sparks of exceptional genius, decided to remove him from his regular studies with the "ma'ari" (the local children's teacher) and began to dedicate long hours each day to intensive Torah study with him.[2, 8] As a sign of supreme protection and success in his studies, the grandfather gave him a sacred silver talisman upon which holy names were engraved.[4]

After the grandfather's death, the youth went to study with the famous righteous men of Yemen at that time.[2, 5] The Kabbalist Rabbi Chayim Yichya Sinuwani, head of the rabbinical court in the nearby city of San'wan, adopted the youth, raised him, and transmitted to him the foundations of the study of the revealed and the esoteric.[2, 5, 7] Subsequently, the youth deepened his knowledge with the head of the rabbinical court in Sha'rab, Rabbi Salim Sa'id.[2, 7]

Already at the age of fourteen, the young man was forced to serve as a "ma'ari" himself in the city of Jabal Habashi in order to support himself, but he did not cease studying.[2, 7] Subsequently, he relocated to the port city of Aden, where he was absorbed into the yeshiva of the head of the Kabbalists of Aden, Rabbi Meshomer Nissim.[1, 2] At the mere age of fifteen, the Rabbi successfully passed comprehensive and rigorous examinations in Gemara, in the books of Rambam, in the Tur and in the Shulchan Arukh, and was formally ordained as a rabbi.[1, 5]

Upon reaching marriageable age, he married the Rabbanit Leah.[1, 2] Immediately after their marriage, the couple made a joint and exceptional decision to dedicate their lives solely to the occupation of Torah, with complete abstention from any engagement in "calculations of human affairs," namely—livelihood and matters of this world.[2, 7] The couple settled in the isolated village of Itzwihah, where Rabbi Sharabi deepened his study of Kabbalah, and his name began to spread throughout the region as a holy man and miracle worker.[2, 7]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Immigration to the Land of Israel and Acclimatization in Jerusalem

In the year 5691 (1931) or 5692 (1932), Rabbi Sharabi decided to immigrate to the Land of Israel.[1, 2] The beginning of his path in the Land was accompanied by severe physical absorption difficulties.[2, 7] He first arrived at the port of Jaffa and from there continued to the city of Rehovot.[2, 3] In Rehovot, he was forced to work in arduous manual labor in the orchards—physically hard work to which he had never been accustomed in Yemen and which severely damaged his ability to concentrate on Torah study.[2, 7]

Out of aspiration to connect to the Torah center of the Holy Land, he decided to relocate to Jerusalem.[2, 7] In Jerusalem, a significant turning point occurred in his economic and Torah life when he received regular financial support from Dr. Moshe Wallach, the legendary director of Sha'arei Tzedek Hospital.[2, 7] This support freed Rabbi Sharabi from the burdens of livelihood and enabled him to immerse himself completely in the study of the revealed and the esoteric.[2, 7]

In Jerusalem, he chose to change his original family name "Yifet" to the name "Sharabi," both after the city of Sha'rab where he acquired his wisdom in Yemen, and because this name carried within it a deep spiritual meaning as an allusion and as an acronym of the verse: Shalom Rav Al Bnei Yisrael.[2, 6, 8]

Rabbi Sharabi's integration into the Jerusalem Kabbalist community was extremely rapid.[2, 7] He began to study at the famous Kabbalist yeshiva Beit El, where he was exceptionally befriended by the head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Shalom Hedaya (father of Rabbi Ovadiah Hedaya).[2, 7] Simultaneously, he established close ties with the head of the Kabbalists in Jerusalem at that time, Rabbi Shaul Dwek HaKohen, and studied with the Jerusalem Kabbalist Rabbi Ya'akov Lopes.[2, 6]

By virtue of his extensive erudition, Rabbi Sharabi began to serve in official teaching positions: he taught Gemara at Yeshivat Sha'arei Rachamim and esoteric Torah at Yeshivat Sha'arei Tzion, which was established by the Rishon LeZion, Rabbi Ben-Zion Meir Chai Uziel.[1, 2]

After the War of Independence and the fall of the Jewish Quarter in the year 5708 (1948), the historic yeshiva Beit El was forced to relocate its activity to the Makor Baruch neighborhood.[2, 7] Rabbi Sharabi was asked by the community leaders to continue delivering the central Kabbalah classes there.[2, 7]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Kabbalistic Teaching and Torah Philosophy

The Torah teaching of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi rested upon a harmonious and precise combination between the world of halakha and the esoteric world, with absolute adherence to the system of prayer kavvanot of Rabbi Shalom Mizrachi Sharabi (the holy Rashash).[4, 9] In his eyes, the study of Kabbalah was not a detached theoretical science, but rather a system of practical spiritual work whose purpose was to effect supreme cosmic rectification, the elevation of sparks of holiness, and the unification of the upper worlds through the letters and words of prayer.[9, 10]

His Daily Routine and Spiritual Work

Rabbi Sharabi's daily routine was demanding and meticulously ordered in an extreme manner, designed to bring body and soul to constant elevation and refinement:

Before dawn: Delivery of deep and complex lessons in esoteric Torah to the select group of Kabbalists.[4]

Shacharit prayer: A long and strenuous prayer at sunrise, recited word by word with precise intention regarding all the unifications of Names and Sefirot appearing in the siddur of the Rashash.[4]

After prayer: Conducting regular and orderly study designed to connect the esoteric to the practical revealed; the study included reading and analysis of the books of Rambam, the Tur with the commentary of the Beit Yosef, and the daily study order of Chok LeYisrael.[4]

Afternoon hours: Delivery of a second comprehensive lesson in esoteric Torah.[4]

Midnight: Performance of Tikkun Chatzot with weeping and enormous supplications.[11, 12] The Rabbi would sit at the threshold of his house, weep bitterly over the exile of the Shekhinah, over the destruction of the Temple and over the troubles of the collective and individual of the people of Israel, while delivering sermons filled with yearnings for the complete redemption.[12]

Rabbi Sharabi was known as possessing an inconceivable phenomenal memory; he had complete mastery of the entire breadth of Torah, and was extraordinarily versed not only in Kabbalah, but also in the wisdom of physiognomy, reincarnation of souls, astronomy, and medicine.[4] His students recounted that every complex difficulty that arose during the study
and he knew how to resolve [difficulties] orally and immediately.[4] Only in exceptional cases did he request that the Sefer ha-Zohar be brought before him, and by pointing to a short and specific passage within it he would reconcile and explain profound difficulties in the words of the Ari, z"l.[4]

The rabbi was most scrupulous in matters of purity, and sharply opposed those who prevent or impede their students from daily immersion in the mikveh.[4] In his final years, when he was compelled to obey the physicians' instructions and refrain from immersion for health reasons, he meticulously observed in his home with piety the enactment of the Ari, z"l—washing the hands forty times continuously while concentrating on special kabbalistic unifications and letter-combinations whose purpose was to attain that same degree of purity as the mikveh.[4]

Rabbi Shara'bi firmly opposed engagement in practical Kabbalah.[4] He spoke sharply against people who use holy names, write amulets based on angelic adjurations, or attempt to coerce physical reality with magical instruments.[4] He believed that salvations must come solely through pure prayer, acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, charity, and the performance of pure pidyon nefesh according to the kavvanot of the Rashash.[13, 14]

His pedagogical and spiritual outlook found expression in an encounter with a young married scholar who studied Kabbalah and wished to know where the most appropriate place was to delve deeply into esoteric works.[4] Rabbi Shara'bi instructed him to go to Breslav Hasidism, explaining: "There is your place, where you can truly be God-fearing and study Kabbalah in the proper way."[4] This statement demonstrates his conception that the study of Kabbalah requires first and foremost a stable spiritual foundation of fear of Heaven, wholeness, and awakening of the heart—qualities well developed in Breslav thought.

The Prayer of the Rashash and Opposition to Leaving the Land of Israel

An integral part of the spiritual teaching that Rabbi Shara'bi transmitted to his students was devotion to a special prayer composed by the holy Rashash.[15] In this prayer the kabbalist describes with great emotion and weeping the sorrow of the Shekhinah in her exile.[15] The essence of the prayer deals with a fervent request of the Creator to merit a good dwelling in the Land of Israel, to study Torah for its own sake without distractions, and above all—a request not to leave the Land of Israel for abroad, and not even to leave the boundaries of Jerusalem for outside Jerusalem.[15, 16] The kabbalists who follow the path of Rabbi Shara'bi were careful, following his words and this instruction, not to leave the borders of the Land under any circumstances whatsoever.[15]

Teachers and Spiritual Influences in the Life Journey of Rabbi Shara'bi

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Yeshivat Nahar Shalom and Its Chain of Transmission

In the year 5722 (1962) Rabbi Shara'bi established the kabbalists' yeshiva "Nahar Shalom" in Jerusalem, named after the divine kabbalist Rabbi Shalom Shara'bi (the Rashash) and after his famous composition.[1, 2, 7] The yeshiva was established in the heart of the Nahalat neighborhood (at the intersection of Shiloh and Zikhron Toviyah streets), and quickly became one of the leading and most important centers in the world for the study of the wisdom of Kabbalah.[17, 18, 19]

The establishment of the yeshiva was accompanied by various local stories.[20] One of the best known among them is connected to the establishment of the adjacent "Binyan Ayni," which was intended to be a multi-story building.[20] According to local tradition, Rabbi Shara'bi discovered that the tall structure would block the sunlight from the yeshiva building and harm the spiritual atmosphere, and he imposed a stricture upon it; since then the building has been considered by neighborhood residents as "cursed" due to the delays and many troubles that befell its builders and residents.[20]

After the passing of Rabbi Shara'bi on 20 Heshvan 5744 (1983), leadership of the yeshiva passed to the kabbalist Rabbi Shalom Aharon Shemu'eli, who was one of the rabbi's outstanding students.[6, 19] Today the yeshiva is headed by his son, the kabbalist Rabbi Beniyahu Shemu'eli, who continues to lead the yeshiva institutions, to hold classes and Friday night study at midnight, and to conduct the historic pidyon nefesh rectifications.[11, 21, 22]

The Enterprise of the Siddur "Reḥovot ha-Nahar"

One of the most significant contributions of Yeshivat Nahar Shalom to the modern kabbalistic world is the editing and printing of the kavvanot prayer book "Reḥovot ha-Nahar."[23] This project, led by the current head of the yeshiva Rabbi Beniyahu Shemu'eli together with a team of Torah scholars from the yeshiva, brought about a veritable revolution in the accessibility of the prayer of those who concentrate [on mystical intentions].[23]

The kabbalistic prayer books based on the system of the Rashash were traditionally written in manuscript only, since old printing was unable to cope with the visual complexity of the prayer book.[23] In these prayer books there is frequent use of special signs: half-letters, inverted letters, letters intertwined one within another, and more.[23] The printing of the first printed prayer book in the year 5670 (1909) was fraught with serious errors; the printer, who did not understand the meaning of the broken and halved letters (which were entirely intentional), corrected them artificially and made them into whole letters, such as for example the letter alef in the word "tzeva'ot" which is supposed to be halved, and thereby damaged the intention of the Name.[23]

The transition to modern word processors enabled the yeshiva editors to accurately reconstruct all the unusual and halved letters, and to integrate the prayer intentions and unifications directly within the sequence of the prayer's words.[23] In the old printed prayer books, the Amidah prayer appeared only once, and the worshiper was forced to flip constantly to other sources to find the intentions for the Sabbath or festival.[23] The use of word processing allowed the prayer to be replicated so that each prayer book contains the complete prayer in its order without need for flipping.[23] The only disadvantage of this method is the breaking up of the historical prayer book (which contained only 4 volumes) into a massive array of approximately 25 separate volumes covering all the prayers of the year.[23]

The Kabbalistic Color System in the Siddur "Reḥovot ha-Nahar"

His Social Conduct and Public Work

Rabbi Mordekhai Shara'bi was not a detached kabbalist sitting in his narrow chamber; his figure was deeply involved in the lives of ordinary people.[3, 6] His modest home on Shiloh Street in the Mahaneh Yehudah neighborhood was wide open at all hours of the day and night to every downtrodden person, sick person, or seeker of advice and blessing.[3, 5, 6]

Love for the Children of Israel and Concern for Their Future

A central and moving dimension of Rabbi Shara'bi's personality was his enormous love for the children of Israel and marginalized youth in Jerusalem.[1, 6] The rabbi, who was not blessed with offspring of his own, saw these children as his spiritual sons.[19, 20] He dedicated his time to teaching children and youths Torah, Mishnayot, and halakhot without receiving any payment.[6]

In addition, the rabbi customarily distributed money and pocket money to youths from the funds that flowed to his home from donations.[1] He did this out of profound educational wisdom in order to attract their hearts to Torah study and to prevent them from wandering the streets of Jerusalem without purpose.[1]

Rabbanit Le'ah Shara'bi: Full Partner in Leadership

At the rabbi's side stood his wife, Rabbanit Le'ah Shara'bi, who was a full partner in his ascetic and simple way of life.[1, 3] Rabbanit Le'ah was an independent figure, socially active and a famous preacher among the women of Jerusalem.[1] She managed the open house and assisted the rabbi in distributing charity funds to the needy.[1, 3]

The rabbanit passed away on 21 Shevat 5738 (1978) [7] (or in the year 5739, 1979).[1] Her passing caused Rabbi Shara'bi profound sorrow, and from then a severe and marked deterioration occurred in his state of health, until his passing on 20 Heshvan 5744 (1983).[1, 7]

Miracles, Pidyon Nefesh, and Relationships with the Great Figures of the Generation

Rabbi Shara'bi was known as a miracle-worker whose blessings and prayers brought about physical changes among seriously ill and hopeless patients.[1, 3] Among dozens of stories, one documented case involves a Jew who came to him with X-ray images before a complicated surgery.[5] The rabbi looked at the images and instructed him to donate 12,000 lira to charity, with a promise that he would not need surgery.[5] The patient immediately wrote the check, and when he returned to the hospital for pre-surgical examinations, the physicians were amazed to discover that the findings had
and islands disappeared entirely.[5]

One of the central instruments that Rabbi Sharabi employed to effect salvations was the secret of the pidyon nefesh (soul redemption) of the Rashash.[13, 14, 21] This pidyon is considered the ultimate kabbalistic remedy for every distress, illness, or harsh decree that threatens the collective or the individual.[13, 14]

The foundations of the pidyon are rooted in the writings of the Ari and the Raḥ"v in Sha'ar ha-Kavvanot (Gate of Intentions), according to which one who performs this pidyon on the eve of Rosh Hashanah and on the eve of Yom Kippur is assured that he will complete his year.[13, 14] The holy Rashash consolidated the tikkun (ritual correction) and established that it should be performed by means of a donation of 160 perutot of pure silver.[14] The number 160 was chosen because its gematria equals the words "tzelem" and "etz" (alluding to the verse "for man is a tree of the field").[14] The pure metals and the holy names that are concentrated upon during the counting of the perutot act to sweeten the gevurot (stern judgments) and dinim (judgments) at their supernal root.[13, 14] Rabbi Sharabi possessed the precise tradition for performing this pidyon, and this merit continues to exist to this day at Yeshivat Nahar Shalom through his disciples.[13, 21]

The esteem of the Rishon Le-Tzion, Maran Rabbi Ovadiah Yosef, for Rabbi Sharabi was immense.[5, 12] Rabbi Ovadiah, who studied with him, defined him in these words: "He was the greatest of the generation, and there was none like him in Kabbalah."[5, 12] A unique spiritual bond also existed between him and the divine Moroccan mekubal, Rabbi Yisrael Abuhatzeira (the "Baba Sali").[12] At one of their meetings, the Baba Sali requested that Rabbi Sharabi reveal to him the root of his soul.[12] After Rabbi Sharabi performed a kabbalistic "she'elat ḥalom" (dream inquiry), he announced to the Baba Sali at their second meeting that the root of his soul emanated from the soul of Hezekiah, King of Judah.[12]

Prominent Disciples and Continuators of Rabbi Sharabi's Path

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Literary Legacy of Rabbi Sharabi

The literary legacy of Rabbi Sharabi is divided into two main channels that reflect the two aspects of his house of study: the world of nigleh (exoteric study) and popular guidance on the one hand, and the world of nistar (esoteric study) and practical kavvanot on the other.[23, 25]

The rabbi's central composition, which was published in three volumes (comprising approximately 980 pages), is called Tefillah le-Moshe (Prayer for Moses).[25, 26] This book constitutes a unique encyclopedia that centralizes a comprehensive collection of tales of righteous individuals, prayers of the ancients, proven medicinal segulot (remedies), practical advice, and ethical guidance that illuminates the path of man.[25, 26, 27] Among other contents, the book contains unique prayers that Rabbi Sharabi himself composed or collected from the writings of the ancients, such as a prayer for business success, a prayer for success in legal proceedings, and focused prayers for the healing of various bodily organs.[27] The book is considered a useful tool in every Jewish home seeking assistance and spiritual well-being in times of distress.[28]

Concurrently, Yeshivat Nahar Shalom continues to publish, under the leadership of Rabbi Binyahu Shmueli, the revolutionary kavvanot siddur Reḥovot ha-Nahar (Streets of the River) and the edition of the Zohar ha-Yomi ha-Mevo'ar (The Annotated Daily Zohar) (comprising dozens of volumes).[21, 23] These literary projects constitute the realization of Rabbi Sharabi's great vision—making the wisdom of nistar and the study of the Zohar accessible to all segments of the people, with the aim of hastening the complete redemption with mercy and without suffering.[10, 21]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Summary: The Legacy of the Doyen of the Mekubalim

The findings of the survey and historical analysis of the figure of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi point to a type of spiritual leadership unique in its kind.[1, 6] The rabbi succeeded in bridging immense cultural and sociological gaps: he elevated the Yemenite kabbalistic heritage and integrated it into the Sephardic-Jerusalemite tradition of the mekubalim of Yeshivat Beit El, while earning absolute veneration both from Hasidic rebbes (such as the Admor of Belz) and from Sephardic halakhic giants (such as Maran Rabbi Ovadiah Yosef).[1, 2, 19]

His personal life, which was marked by orphanhood, poverty, and the absence of children of his own, did not transform him into a recluse or an embittered person.[4, 19] On the contrary—he and his wife, Rebbetzin Leah, translated their personal pain into immense love and paternal concern for every needy person, youth, and child in Jerusalem, while maintaining an ascetic lifestyle and renouncing every trace of personal material pleasure.[1, 3, 6]

His literary and institutional legacy, represented today by the yeshiva of mekubalim Nahar Shalom, continues to operate at full strength.[21, 22] The project of printing computerized kavvanot siddurim and disseminating the Zohar to the masses constitutes the fulfillment of the life vow of one who changed his name to "Sharabi" in order to bear upon his shoulders in prayer great peace for the Children of Israel.[1, 6, 23]

# The Journey of a Luminary: Stations in the Life and Legacy of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi zt"l

The figure of Rabbenu Mordechai Sharabi zt"l (1912–1984) stands as a pillar of fire before the camp, a wondrous spiritual bridge connecting the ancient mystical traditions of Shar'ab in Yemen with the alleyways of the new Jerusalem. As "Elder of the Kabbalists" and "Chief of the Mekhavvenim," the Rabbi embodied a rare combination of humility covering infinite greatness, phenomenal erudition in both the revealed and concealed realms of Torah, and love of Israel that broke through all barriers. His journey is a story of transcendence beyond material limitations and the transformation of personal orphanhood into spiritual fatherhood for an entire generation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Yemenite Roots: Between Orphanhood and Sanctity (1912–1931)

The Rabbi was born in the city of Shar'ab in Yemen to Mirat Miriam and Rabbi Yehudah Yefet-Ta'izi. The dawn of his life was darkened by double tragedy: his father died before he was born, and his mother passed away when he was only about two years old. The young child was raised in the home of his grandfather, Rabbi Avraham Yefet Ta'izi, who served as Av Beit Din of Shar'ab. The grandfather was a holy man who, according to tradition, employed kefitzat haderekh (miraculous travel) to visit Jerusalem. Precisely in this impoverished household, under the threat of the "Orphans' Decree"—a cruel royal law mandating the forced conversion of Jewish orphans to Islam—the young prodigy flourished. The constant fear of apostasy did not weaken his resolve; on the contrary, it propelled him to immerse himself in the sanctuary of Torah.

The tension between material poverty and spiritual strength:

Educational milestones in Yemen:

Age 8: Appointed by the sages of his city as "Mar'i d'Ar'a," disseminating Torah to the masses.

Age 15: Successfully passed comprehensive examinations on the entire Shas, Arba'ah Turim, and Mishneh Torah of the Rambam, and was ordained for the rabbinate.

Holy practices: Despite being delicate in constitution, he maintained daily immersion in broken mikva'ot and observed uninterrupted fasts from Saturday night until Friday night.

The spiritual wealth he accumulated in Yemen was like an ever-strengthening spring, but his early revelation of greatness brought him into contact with figures who became foundation stones in the edifice of his spiritual stature.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Formative Figures and the Beginning of the Spiritual Journey

The Rabbi's world was shaped under the guidance of spiritual giants in Yemen. The defining encounter occurred when the mekubbal Rabbi Hayyim Sinuani observed the boy Mordechai leading a donkey for a merchant while holding a book and studying with immense concentration as he walked. Rabbi Sinuani recognized the divine spark, "purchased" the boy from the merchant, and adopted him as a son and disciple.

The exemplary figures who built his world:

Rabbi Hayyim Sinuani: The first guide who introduced him to the gates of the PaRDeS (esoteric Torah). He cultivated Rabbi Mordechai and transmitted to him the foundations of mystical Torah with great depth.

Rabbi Salim Sa'id: The rabbi of the city of Shar'ab, who recognized the boy's greatness and took him to the city of al-Hada to serve alongside him and absorb his ways of conduct.

Rabbi Meshumer Nissim: Head of the mekubbalim in the city of Aden, to whom the Rabbi moved in his youth. Under his aegis, the Rabbi deepened his knowledge of the kavvanot (mystical intentions) of the Nistar (concealed Torah) before his ascent to the Land.

The decision to ascend to Eretz Yisrael crystallized following a turbulent event: the ruler of Yemen fabricated a blood libel against the community over money stolen from him. The Rabbi employed the goral ha-hitpofel (divination through random text selection) and revealed the hiding place of the money, but immediately thereafter fled to the Holy Land for fear that the regime would compel him to use practical Kabbalah for its purposes—a path the Rabbi utterly abhorred.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. The Journey to Holiness: From Aden to Jerusalem (1931–1932)

The journey to Eretz Yisrael was fraught with dangers. The Rabbi and his wife Leah fled secretly from Yemen to Aden, and from there sailed via Port Said in Egypt to the port of Jaffa. Upon descending to the shore in 1931, the Rabbi prostrated himself on the soil of the Land and kissed its earth while weeping.

In Jerusalem, the Rabbi chose to change his family name to Sharabi. This was not merely a commemoration of his birthplace Shar'ab, but a spiritual declaration of intent in acronym form: Shalom Rav 'al Benei Yisra'el (abundant peace upon the children of Israel).

After a brief period during which the Rabbanit Leah tried to support them so that the Rabbi could devote himself to his Torah study, the couple settled in a poor and cramped room in the Mahane Yehudah neighborhood, a place that quickly became a locus of sanctity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

4. The Period of Establishment in Jerusalem: Yeshivat Beit El and the Revelation of Greatness

Initially, the Rabbi lived in abject poverty in a small room in the Rahamim synagogue, where he delivered classes to the public. He began studying at the yeshivah of mekubbalim Beit El, where he sat on the side as a simple Jew. His greatness was revealed "by chance" at Yeshivat Matteh Ya'akov: Rabbi Ya'akov Lopez presented an enormous difficulty in the writings of Etz Hayyim; Rabbi Sharabi, in humility, left a hidden note with the solution. When the note was discovered, the sages of Jerusalem understood that a spiritual giant was concealed among them. The Rosh Yeshivah, Rabbi Shalom Hedaya zt"l, immediately adopted him as the successor to the lineage of mekhavvenim of the Rashash.

Holy practices and mortifications:

Minimal sleep: Adherence to only 20 minutes of sleep per day on a simple pallet.

Immersion and sanctity: When prevented from immersing in a mikveh due to his health, he would perform netilat yadayim of the Ari 40 times with kavanah.

Uninterrupted fasts: Continuous fasting from Saturday night until Friday night for six years.

Midnight study: Performing tikkun hatzot and studying kavvanot every night in darkness and with weeping.

His establishment as a supreme authority within existing institutions prepared him to establish an independent sanctuary for mystical Torah, especially after the destruction of the Old City in 1948.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

5. Establishment of Yeshivat Nahar Shalom and Leadership as "Chief of the Mekhavvenim"

In 1962, the Rabbi established the yeshivah of mekubbalim Nahar Shalom in Nahla'ot. The Rabbi feared that the chain of mekhavvenim according to the siddur of the Rashash would be severed, and he transformed the yeshivah into the world center for disseminating Kabbalah in its purity. The Rabbi utterly nullified his ego and demanded this of his students, while opening the gates of study also to the younger generation.

Characteristics of the approach:

Nullification of ego: Study of Kabbalah as a tool for refinement of character traits and not for attaining honor.

Accessibility with reverence: Making Kabbalah accessible to all who are prepared to toil in purity, out of desire to hasten the redemption.

Prayer in "the name of all Israel": Emphasis that every spiritual action is performed in the name of the entire nation.

The spiritual daily schedule in the yeshivah:

His stature as Chief of the Mekhavvenim did not disconnect him from the people; on the contrary, he became the "Western Wall" of all the Jews of the Land.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

6. The Leader of All: Kindness, Simplicity, and Wonders

Rabbi Sharabi eschewed all honorifics and luxuries. When the Hasidim of Belz offered him a spacious residence, he firmly refused. For him, physical luxury was a barrier and partition preventing the spiritual concentration required of a mekhaven. He championed the approach of "pleasant ways" and preferred the path of Rav Kook over extremist zealotry, saying: "Rav Kook brought the distant near, and this is our way!"

Wonders of outreach and spiritual heroism:

The motorcycle on Shabbat: When a secular youth rode beside him publicly, the Rabbi said with compassion: "The motorcycle is at fault, not the young man." After the motorcycle expired, the Rabbi invited the youth to a Shabbat meal, and thereafter the motorcycle (and its owner) began observing Shabbat.

The spiritual "Chief of Staff": His students called him thus because of his devotion to the welfare of IDF soldiers. He saw the physical defense of the Land as a direct result of the spiritual "war" in the kavvanot of prayer.

The pilot's vision: During the daring Operation Yayin, the helicopter pilot recounted that he saw the figure of an old man encouraging him to continue flying despite the weight of the stolen Egyptian radar; the pilot later identified the figure of Rabbi Sharabi as the form he saw in his vision.

"Before anything one does or studies, one should say: 'I hereby am studying in the name of all Israel.' Through this one effects a tremendous rectification and elevates the Shekhinah, and accomplishes the clarification in all the worlds." (From the practices of Rabbenu)
7. Conclusion: The Eternal Legacy (1983 Onwards)

The Rabbi ascended in a heavenly storm on the 20th of Ḥeshvan 5744. His funeral was among the largest Jerusalem had known, and symbolized the unity of the people around him. The Baba Sali, of blessed memory, testified that Rabbi Sharabi sacrificed his life as atonement for the generation in order to nullify a harsh decree he had sensed through his holy spirit.

Provisions for the Journey – Insights for Life from the Legacy of Rabbi Sharabi:

Humility as a Receptive Vessel: True greatness has no need for grand halls. The simplicity of the home is the key to purity of thought.

Unconditional Love of Israel: To see in every Jew, even the most distant, a "lofty soul" whose light is merely concealed by materiality.

Human Effort: Mastery is not a miracle, but the fruit of infinite repetition and devotion to purpose.

Universal Mission: Every private act of a person must be performed "in the name of all Israel" in order to grant it eternal significance.

May his memory be blessed and may his merit protect us. Amen.

Architecture of Spiritual Leadership: A Strategic Analysis of the Figure of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi

1. Introduction: The Dual Model of Leadership and Socio-Spiritual Synthesis

The figure of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi, of blessed memory, is not merely a glorious chapter in the historiography of Yemenite Jewry, but constitutes a critical "test case" for analyzing the architecture of spiritual leadership in the modern era. For professionals in the fields of the rabbinate and community, Rabbi Sharabi offers a unique model of socio-spiritual synthesis: the capacity to convert abstract kabbalistic attainments and ascetic withdrawal into concrete social action at the heart of Israeli existence.

As "Dean of the Kabbalists" and "Head of the Community of Kavvanim," Rabbi Sharabi was not content with preserving the tradition of the past. His leadership strategy began with an ontological declaration of intent – changing his family name to Sharabi, an acronym for Shalom Rav 'Al Benei Yisra'el (Great Peace Upon the Children of Israel). Thereby he defined the purpose of the leader's existence: not the accumulation of power or honor, but the transformation of the spiritual entity into an instrument serving to establish peace in the nation. His roots in the Yemenite realm, which grew out of dual orphanhood and deprivation, laid the foundation for an internal strength that enabled him to progress from personal survival under harsh decrees to large-scale community building in the Land of Israel.

2. Roots of Growth: The "Aḥitofel Lottery" and Metaphysical Responsibility

Rabbi Sharabi's leadership was forged in the crucible of Yemenite exile. His early orphanhood (his father, R. Yehudah, died before his birth; his mother, Miriam, died when he was two years old) and upbringing under the threat of the "Orphans' Decree" created in him a rare psychological resilience. The formative encounter with Rabbi Ḥayyim Sinuani revealed an "architecture of concentration": a child leading a donkey in the desert, holding a book in one hand and studying amid the jolting of the journey.

The strategic turning point that precipitated his aliyah to the Land (1931) was the "Aḥitofel Lottery" incident. When an accusation of theft was leveled against the Jewish community by the local ruler, the Rabbi used kabbalistic tools to expose the thieves and save the nation. However, as a leader understanding the danger in using "practical Kabbalah," the Rabbi chose to flee to the Land of Israel in order to prevent a situation where he would be compelled to use these powers again for immediate needs. This action demonstrates metaphysical responsibility: the leader identifies the boundary between miracle and necessity, and chooses emigration as a tool for protecting the purity of his spiritual role.

3. Sacred Service as the Backbone of Authority: The Architecture of the Night

The Rabbi's public authority derived not from official appointment, but from an "architecture of holiness" – extreme self-discipline that made him a focal point of power. His daily regimen included only 20 minutes of sleep (22:00-22:20), study from midnight, and "interruption" fasts that continued for six consecutive years. The "why" behind the mortifications was clear: refinement of the leadership vessel. The leader mortifies his body in order to expand his capacity to contain the suffering of the public.

The Core of Nocturnal Study – The Nine Foundational Books: Each night the Rabbi studied nine basic books that shaped his consciousness: Divrei Shalom, Zohar, Ṭur, Beit Yosef, Mishneh Torah of Maimonides, 'Etz Ḥayyim, Pele Yo'etz, Shulḥan 'Arukh, and Sha'ar Ruaḥ ha-Kodesh (or Tikkune Zohar).

4. The "Nahar Shalom" Yeshiva: Strategic Preservation of the Mekhavennim Dynasty

The establishment of the "Nahar Shalom" yeshiva in the Naḥla'ot neighborhood was not merely a religious act, but a strategic move for preserving tradition. After the destruction of the "Beit El" yeshiva in the Old City in 1948, the Rabbi identified the danger of severing the mekhavennim dynasty of the Rashash. The yeshiva became a "power station" that radiated to the entire surrounding area.

The Economic Architecture of the Kabbalist's Court: The Rabbi implemented a unique economic model: "zero personal profit." He never demanded payment for his blessings, and in cases where he received donations, these were immediately channeled to support Torah scholars, aid the needy, and provide "advancement funds" (gemach) to youths for reciting Psalms and Mishnayot. The leader functions as a "conduit for resource transfer" – he does not accumulate wealth, but redirects it to channels of social construction.

5. The Leader as Systemic Mediator: De-Personalization of Sin and Spiritual Healing

Rabbi Sharabi's leadership capacity was evident in his psychological-spiritual approach to conflict resolution.

De-Personalization Strategy: In the famous story of the youth and the motorcycle on Shabbat, the Rabbi declared: "He is not guilty, the motorcycle is guilty." In strategic analysis, this is a move of detaching the sin from the sinner. By placing blame on the object, the Rabbi removed the youth's internal resistance and enabled him a path of repentance born of love.

Systemic Healing: The use of "remedies" such as bananas or the story of "The Doves in the Hospital" (the jaundice cure of R. Yehudah Motzafi) is not simple magic. This is an understanding of spiritual roots for physical illnesses. The leader functions as a "systems engineer" performing a repair at the hidden level in order to achieve a result at the manifest level.

Sublimation of Fatherhood: The Rabbi and his wife Leah were childless for approximately fifty years. Rather than withdrawing inward, the Rabbi performed a sublimation of paternal emotion and became "father of the generation." His infinite concern for orphans and youths was an expression of the leader's capacity to rise above his personal deficiency and transform it into an engine of pan-national giving.

6. The National Interface: The "Eastern Wall" of the Nation

Rabbi Sharabi held an active national conception, clearly choosing the "pleasant ways" approach of Rabbi Kook. He determined that Rabbi Kook brought the distant near and that this was the way one must follow.

Practical and Spiritual Zionism: In his home was hidden a weapons cache of the Etzel, and he was meticulous about prayers for the peace of the State and the IDF soldiers. The testimony about his weeping at night over the peace of soldiers at the front reveals a leader feeling total responsibility for the physical security of the State.

Junction of Leaders: His relationship with the "Baba Sali" (who asked the Rabbi to determine the root of his soul and received the answer: King Ḥizkiyah) and the appreciation of Rabbi Ovadiah Yosef (who testified that he was "the greatest of the generation" in Kabbalah), position him as the "Eastern Wall" – a place where all streams meet.

7. Summary: Core Principles for Leadership (Strategic Takeaways)

From the analysis of Rabbi Sharabi's figure emerge five "directives" for professional spiritual leadership:

Ego Nullification as the Basis for Authority: Public authority is built from extreme self-refinement (Ego-Nullification).

The establishment of institutions as a cultural "Noah's Ark."

Leadership without coercion (the 'motorcycle' strategy): Using gentle ways and detaching blame from the person to enable internal change.

Metaphysical responsibility as Atonement: The leader sees himself as "atonement" for the generation. The story in which he "gave his life" to annul a decree that the Baba Sali sensed is the pinnacle of leadership architecture—the leader as human/spiritual shield.

Unity through accessibility: Transforming the home and yeshiva into an open space without barriers between streams ("the Eastern Wall").

True leadership is not measured by dominion, but by the ability to transform personal holiness into a social address. Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi proved that the depth of the hidden is the engine for outreach in the revealed. We, as community leaders, must adopt the model that combines unceasing diligence with unconditional love of Israel, to ensure that the voice of the "rav shalom" continues to resonate upon all the children of Israel.

Institutional Impact Report: Yeshivat "Nahar Shalom"—Between Yeshiva Kabbalah and Social Leadership

1. Introduction: The Transition from Yemen to Jerusalem and Laying the Spiritual Cornerstone

The founding of Yeshivat "Nahar Shalom" in Jerusalem constitutes a formative chapter in the sociology of Sephardic Jewry in the twentieth century, as it represents a transition from passive preservation of tradition in Yemen to active institutional establishment at the heart of the Israeli space. The yeshiva was founded as a strategic bridge designed to preserve the legacy of the kabbalist the Rashash (Rabbi Shalom Sharabi), while dynamically adapting it to the needs of the developing Jerusalem neighborhoods, thereby ensuring the vitality of esoteric Torah as a living component of communal identity.

Analysis of the roots: The founder, Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi, was born in Yemen as Mordechai Yefet-Ta'izi (circa 1912). His life trajectory, from his early orphanhood and studies with Rabbi Haim Sinwani—who recognized his unique diligence while he was still leading donkeys in the desert—to his ordination at age 15 by Rabbi Meshomer Nissim, shaped a figure combining phenomenal expertise in both the revealed and the hidden. His arrival in Jerusalem in 1932 marked the beginning of an institutional transformation: from spiritual solitude to public leadership.

The institutional vision: The choice of the name "Nahar Shalom" (after the Rashash's composition) and the change of the family name to "Sharabi" were not merely symbolic steps, but rather institutional rebranding. The name Sharabi is interpreted as an acronym expressing social mission: "shalom rav al benei Yisrael" (great peace upon the children of Israel). Thereby the institution defined its purpose as a center designed to influence the broader public sphere and not only the scholarly elite group.

Connectivity: This process transformed the yeshiva from another neighborhood study hall in Nahalat into a nationwide center of attraction, where the founder's charismatic personality was translated into a stable institutional structure.

2. The Spiritual Architecture of Yeshivat "Nahar Shalom"

"Nahar Shalom" functioned as a unique center for applied kabbalah (kavvanot), a model considered innovative and pioneering in its period. While other kabbalist yeshivot tended toward insularity, the institution led a process of "democratization of the esoteric," while making the complex esoteric Torah accessible to the broader public.

The core of religious-research activity: The institution established a rigid study discipline based on the Rashash's siddur and Sefer Etz Hayyim. The flagship project—editing and distributing the "Reḥovot HaNahar" siddurim—transformed the Rashash's kavvanot from hidden manuscripts into a standardized and accessible institutional "product." Rabbi Sharabi functioned as a living database; his students testified that he could correct their precise pronunciation in the kavvanot from memory alone, without need of a book, thereby ensuring the accuracy of the oral tradition in an era of transition to printed text.

The institutional daily schedule as a model for discipline:

Midnight: Beginning of activity with "tikkun ḥatzot" and unique kavvanot.

Pre-dawn study: Kabbalah lessons before dawn.

Vattikin: Morning prayer at sunrise with the Rashash's kavvanot.

Study layers: Lessons in Rambam and Tur constituting a solid halakhic foundation.

Sociological implications: The economic model of the yeshiva—comprehensive avoidance of collecting payment for blessings or spiritual services—created a "spiritual meritocracy." This decoupling between spiritual actions and material incentives produced the institutional legitimacy of the yeshiva among all sectors, from Belz Hasidim to the secular public, and distinguished it from other institutions that absorbed criticism for commercialization of religion.

3. The Institution as Social Anchor: Gemach and Integration of Marginal Youth

The yeshiva functioned as a communal safety net, while adopting an integrative approach that sought to prevent social alienation among Sephardic youth in modernizing Jerusalem.

Economic support mechanisms: The yeshiva operated a significant aid system, which included gemach loans for purchasing apartments (in amounts of approximately $1,000 in contemporary values) and secret support for hidden righteous individuals. The yeshiva served as a node for wealth distribution, where donations were directed directly to solving housing and subsistence crises in the community.

Rehabilitation and integration (the "socio-religious bypass"): In contrast to insular Lithuanian-Ashkenazic models, "Nahar Shalom" operated positive reinforcement mechanisms for identity preservation among youth in distress:

Strategic analysis: The famous story about the motorcycle rider on Shabbat ("it's not his fault, the motorcycle is at fault") demonstrates a strategy of separating the agent (the person) from his actions. This inclusive approach enabled the yeshiva to serve as an effective agent of social change that prevented an intergenerational and communal rupture.

4. The Yeshiva on the Front Lines: Contribution to State Security and Risk Management

The institution's involvement in state security demonstrates bold "institutional risk management" combining national loyalty with spiritual vision.

Risk management vis-à-vis the Mandate: The yeshiva served as a "clearing house" for weapons for the Irgun. The decision was based on a strategic assessment that the British would not suspect a house of worship of kabbalists. This involved taking heavy institutional risk for the benefit of the national struggle.

Institutional tension and IDF service: The institution's position regarding conscription was characterized by built-in tension. The story of the beard changing color to white overnight (following his wife's agreement) in order to appear elderly and prevent forced conscription, emphasizes the institution's perception that its decisive contribution is in the spiritual preservation of the nation. Nevertheless, the institution functioned as a "spiritual headquarters" during wars, when the rabbi performed "tikkun shofarot" and prayers for the safety of soldiers.

Applied kabbalah at the national level: The yeshiva provided responses to physical distress through kabbalah (such as the "pigeon tikkun" for jaundice or the "banana" recommendation for the wounded soldier), thereby transforming kabbalah into a tool of social resilience and public health in times of crisis.

5. Outlook and Ideology: The "Derakhehah Darkhei No'am" Model

The yeshiva's ideology served as a moderating and unifying factor in Israeli society, while preferring Rabbi Kook's approach of outreach over Rabbi Zonnenfeld's separatism.

National-religious bridge: The choice of the "derakhehah darkhei no'am" (her ways are ways of pleasantness) approach was a conscious institutional decision. The yeshiva regularly held prayers for the welfare of the state and IDF soldiers, thereby creating a unique Sephardic identity combining halakhic stringency with spiritual Zionism.

Inter-sectoral junction: The yeshiva functioned as a rare meeting point in the Jerusalem space. Rabbi Sharabi's stature was so exalted that the Baba Sali himself requested that he perform a "she'elah bashamayim" (heavenly inquiry) regarding the root of his soul (and was answered that he is the soul of King Hezekiah). This recognition by other leaders transformed "Nahar Shalom" into a junction bringing together Belz Hasidim, Ashkenazim, Sephardim, and secular Jews around the common denominator of kabbalah.

6. Summary: Continuing Legacy and Long-Term Impact

The survival of Yeshivat "Nahar Shalom" after the founder's death in 1983 constitutes a rare test case of successful transition from "charismatic leadership" to a stable "institutional-bureaucratic structure." Under the leadership of his successor, Rabbi Beniyahu Shmueli, the institution maintained its status as a communal anchor in Nahalat while expanding its nationwide influence.

Components of institutional impact:

Preservation of kavvanot technology: Making the Rashash's kabbalah accessible through standardization of texts and study methods.

Social stability
The creation of mutual aid mechanisms (gemilut ḥasadim) that built the economic resilience of the Naḥla'ot community.

The consolidation of religious-national identity: offering a moderate and unifying alternative that prevented sectarian and communal polarization.

In conclusion, the yeshiva "Nahar Shalom" is not merely an educational institution, but a social-religious organization that functioned as a central axis in shaping modern Jerusalem, while transforming esoteric Kabbalah into an instrument for national and social cohesion.

Study Introduction: The Sacred Paths of Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi z"l

Welcome to an educational journey in the footsteps of one of the most wondrous and influential figures in the kabbalistic world of recent generations. This study sheet will introduce you to Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi, a figure who combined divine depths with simple human humility, and who served as a spiritual bridge for the entire people of Israel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. The Spiritual Compass: Who Was Rabbi Mordechai Sharabi?

Rabbi Mordechai Yehuda Yefet Sharabi was born in Yemen (circa 1908) into a reality of early orphanhood from both parents. His roots were planted in a lineage of sanctity; his grandfather, Rabbi Avraham Yefet-Ta'izi, was a judge (dayyan) and a miraculous man about whom it is recounted that he would employ qefitsah ha-derekh ("shortening of the way") in order to arrive from Yemen to adjudicate in Jerusalem.

Already at age 9, while he was an orphan wandering between villages and teaching Torah, the kabbalist Rabbi Ḥayyim Sinwani encountered him. Rabbi Sinwani was astonished to see a small child leading a donkey with one hand while holding a study text in his other hand, completely immersed in learning. He "acquired" the child from the man accompanying him and became his primary teacher.

"The Rabbi was not merely a Torah scholar; he was 'an angel of the Lord of Hosts,' 'the Western Wall of the people of Israel,' and a shining light in the heart of a confused generation. His figure radiated extreme humility and complete nullification of the 'I' for the sake of communal sanctity."

Insight for the learner: The Rabbi's life teaches us that spiritual greatness is not dependent upon one's material starting point. The small orphan who led a donkey became the "Chief of Staff of prayers," proving that willpower and devotion to Torah can penetrate any difficulty.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. The Secret of the Name and the Lineage: "Great Peace upon the Children of Israel"

The Rabbi saw himself as a link in the lineage of the divine kabbalist the Rashash (Rabbi Shalom Sharabi). Upon his immigration to the Land in 1932, he chose to change his family name to "Sharabi," not only as a connection to his city but as a declaration of spiritual intentions.

For contemplation: For the kabbalist, a name is a work program. Reflect: How does the identity you bear or the appellation by which you are called serve a purpose that is beyond your personal needs?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. The World of Kavvanot and the Siddur "Reḥovot ha-Nahar"

At yeshivat "Nahar Shalom" which he established in Jerusalem, the Rabbi not only taught Kabbalah but embarked upon a national rescue mission. After the destruction of the Old City and the dispersal of yeshivat "Bet El," the Rabbi feared that the chain of mekhavennim (those who know how to unify unifications in prayer) would be severed. He was a staunch supporter of the State of Israel and its soldiers, often praying tearfully for their safety. This support manifested in concrete action; on the eve of the War of Independence, he allowed members of the Etzel underground to hide a cache of weapons in his home. He expressed agreement with the path of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, which emphasized bringing people closer to Judaism with love and gentle encouragement.

He shared this life of service with his first wife, Rabbanit Leah, for over 50 years. Though they were childless, their partnership was one of deep spiritual devotion. Rabbanit Leah was herself a community activist, giving lectures to women and dedicating her life to acts of kindness.

His daily routine was a testament to his relentless spiritual diligence and was structured around near-constant study, prayer, and service.

Immersive Study: He would then learn sacred texts throughout the night until the sunrise prayer (netz). Receiving the Public: After morning prayers and a brief meal, he would dedicate his mornings to the people. Countless individuals from all walks of life flocked to his home for blessings, counsel, and aid, and he received each one with warmth and patience.

Unceasing Prayer: He prayed with the deep Kabbalistic intentions of the Rashash and maintained the custom of wearing two pairs of tefillin (of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam) simultaneously during prayer.
